EP1 ReviewMidterm · Chapters 1–8

Summaryまとめ

Every module of Chapters 1–8 in a few short points, each with a worked example that opens one step at a time, and the common mistakes of each chapter.

Chapter 1 · Modules 1-1 to 1-3

Measurement

1-1Measuring things, including lengths

  • SI units. Mechanics needs three base quantities: length in metres (m), mass in kilograms (kg) and time in seconds (s). Every other unit is built from them, such as 1 N=1 kg⋅m/s2.1\text{ N}=1\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}^2.1 N=1 kg⋅m/s2.
  • Prefixes. k=103\text{k}=10^3k=103, M=106\text{M}=10^6M=106, G=109\text{G}=10^9G=109; c=10−2\text{c}=10^{-2}c=10−2, m=10−3\text{m}=10^{-3}m=10−3, μ=10−6\mu=10^{-6}μ=10−6, n=10−9\text{n}=10^{-9}n=10−9.
  • Changing units. Multiply by conversion factors equal to 111, so the unit you don't want cancels. For areas and volumes, square or cube the factor.
  • Significant figures. A sum or difference keeps the fewest decimal places; a product or quotient keeps the fewest significant figures.
Worked example1-1

Give each answer in SI units, with the right number of significant figures.

  1. (a)A car moves at 72.072.072.0 km/h. Express its speed in m/s.
  2. (b)A sticker has an area of 3.0 cm23.0\text{ cm}^23.0 cm2. Express it in m2\text{m}^2m2.
  3. (c)Add 4.24.24.2 m and 0.1350.1350.135 m.
  4. (d)Multiply 2.502.502.50 m by 0.00400.00400.0040 m.
Show solutionHide solution
Answer
  • (a)20.020.020.0 m/s
  • (b)3.0×10−4 m23.0\times10^{-4}\text{ m}^23.0×10−4 m2
  • (c)4.34.34.3 m
  • (d)0.010 m20.010\text{ m}^20.010 m2

(a) 72.0 kmh×1000 m1 km×1 h3600 s=72 0003600 ms=20.0\displaystyle 72.0\ \frac{\text{km}}{\text{h}}\times\frac{1000\text{ m}}{1\text{ km}}\times\frac{1\text{ h}}{3600\text{ s}}=\frac{72\,000}{3600}\ \frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}=20.072.0 hkm​×1 km1000 m​×3600 s1 h​=360072000​ sm​=20.0 m/s.

(b) 1 cm=10−21\text{ cm}=10^{-2}1 cm=10−2 m, so 1 cm2=(10−2 m)2=10−4 m21\text{ cm}^2=(10^{-2}\text{ m})^2=10^{-4}\text{ m}^21 cm2=(10−2 m)2=10−4 m2 and 3.0 cm2=3.0×10−4 m2.3.0\text{ cm}^2=3.0\times10^{-4}\text{ m}^2.3.0 cm2=3.0×10−4 m2.

(c) 4.2+0.135=4.3354.2+0.135=4.3354.2+0.135=4.335 m, but 4.24.24.2 is only known to the tenths, so the sum is 4.34.34.3 m.

(d) 2.50×0.0040=0.0100 m2.2.50\times0.0040=0.0100\text{ m}^2.2.50×0.0040=0.0100 m2. 0.00400.00400.0040 has two significant figures (leading zeros don't count), so the product is 0.010 m20.010\text{ m}^20.010 m2.

1-2Time

  • The second is defined by an atomic clock: 9 192 631 7709\,192\,631\,7709192631770 oscillations of the light from a cesium-133 atom.
  • The metre is defined by the speed of light, exactly c=299 792 458c=299\,792\,458c=299792458 m/s: one metre is the distance light travels in 1299 792 458\frac{1}{299\,792\,458}2997924581​ s.
  • Time units convert like any other: 1 day=24×3600 s=86 4001\text{ day}=24\times3600\text{ s}=86\,4001 day=24×3600 s=86400 s.
Worked example1-2

Use c≈3.00×108c\approx3.00\times10^8c≈3.00×108 m/s.

  1. (a)How many seconds are there in one day?
  2. (b)How far does light travel in 1.001.001.00 ns?
  3. (c)About how many days is 1.00×1061.00\times10^61.00×106 s?

Answer
  • (a)86 40086\,40086400 s
  • (b)0.3000.3000.300 m (30.030.030.0 cm)
  • (c)About 11.611.611.6 days

(a) 1 day×24 h1 day×3600 s1 h=86 400\displaystyle 1\text{ day}\times\frac{24\text{ h}}{1\text{ day}}\times\frac{3600\text{ s}}{1\text{ h}}=86\,4001 day×1 day24 h​×1 h3600 s​=86400 s.

(b) d=ct=(3.00×108 m/s)(1.00×10−9 s)=0.300d=ct=(3.00\times10^8\text{ m/s})(1.00\times10^{-9}\text{ s})=0.300d=ct=(3.00×108 m/s)(1.00×10−9 s)=0.300 m, about the length of a ruler.

(c) 1.00×106 s86 400 s/day≈11.6\displaystyle \frac{1.00\times10^6\text{ s}}{86\,400\text{ s/day}}\approx11.686400 s/day1.00×106 s​≈11.6 days.

1-3Mass

  • The kilogram is the SI unit of mass. Atoms are weighed in atomic mass units, 1 u=1.66×10−271\text{ u}=1.66\times10^{-27}1 u=1.66×10−27 kg; a carbon-12 atom is exactly 121212 u.
  • Density is mass per unit volume, in kg/m3\text{kg/m}^3kg/m3: ρ=mV\rho=\frac{m}{V}ρ=Vm​ and 1 g/cm3=103 kg/m3.1\text{ g/cm}^3=10^3\text{ kg/m}^3.1 g/cm3=103 kg/m3.
Worked example1-3

An aluminium cube is 2.002.002.00 cm on each side and has a mass of 21.621.621.6 g.

  1. (a)Find its volume in m3\text{m}^3m3.

  4. (d)The cube is melted and drawn into a wire with a cross-section of 1.00 mm21.00\text{ mm}^21.00 mm2. How long is the wire?

  • (b)2.70×103 kg/m32.70\times10^3\text{ kg/m}^32.70×103 kg/m3
  • (c)2.70 g/cm32.70\text{ g/cm}^32.70 g/cm3
  • (d)8.008.008.00 m

(a) V=(2.00 cm)3=8.00 cm3,V=(2.00\text{ cm})^3=8.00\text{ cm}^3,V=(2.00 cm)3=8.00 cm3, and 1 cm3=(10−2 m)3=10−6 m3,1\text{ cm}^3=(10^{-2}\text{ m})^3=10^{-6}\text{ m}^3,1 cm3=(10−2 m)3=10−6 m3, so V=8.00×10−6 m3.V=8.00\times10^{-6}\text{ m}^3.V=8.00×10−6 m3.

(b) m=21.6 g=21.6×10−3m=21.6\text{ g}=21.6\times10^{-3}m=21.6 g=21.6×10−3 kg, so ρ=mV=21.6×10−38.00×10−6=2.70×103 kg/m3.\displaystyle \rho=\frac{m}{V}=\frac{21.6\times10^{-3}}{8.00\times10^{-6}}=2.70\times10^3\text{ kg/m}^3.ρ=Vm​=8.00×10−621.6×10−3​=2.70×103 kg/m3. Both measurements have three significant figures, so the quotient keeps three.

(c) ρ=21.6 g8.00 cm3=2.70 g/cm3.\displaystyle \rho=\frac{21.6\text{ g}}{8.00\text{ cm}^3}=2.70\text{ g/cm}^3.ρ=8.00 cm321.6 g​=2.70 g/cm3. Check 1 g/cm3=10−3 kg10−6 m3=103 kg/m3.\displaystyle 1\text{ g/cm}^3=\frac{10^{-3}\text{ kg}}{10^{-6}\text{ m}^3}=10^3\text{ kg/m}^3.1 g/cm3=10−6 m310−3 kg​=103 kg/m3.

(d) Melting keeps the volume: 8.00 cm3=8.00×103 mm3,8.00\text{ cm}^3=8.00\times10^3\text{ mm}^3,8.00 cm3=8.00×103 mm3, since 1 cm3=(10 mm)3.1\text{ cm}^3=(10\text{ mm})^3.1 cm3=(10 mm)3. Then L=VA=8.00×103 mm31.00 mm2=8.00×103 mm=8.00\displaystyle L=\frac{V}{A}=\frac{8.00\times10^3\text{ mm}^3}{1.00\text{ mm}^2}=8.00\times10^3\text{ mm}=8.00L=AV​=1.00 mm28.00×103 mm3​=8.00×103 mm=8.00 m.

Watch out

  • Converting cm2\text{cm}^2cm2 or cm3\text{cm}^3cm3 with the length factor alone: 1 m2=104 cm2,1\text{ m}^2=10^4\text{ cm}^2,1 m2=104 cm2, not 10210^2102.
  • Rounding in the middle of a calculation. Keep extra digits and round only the final answer.

Chapter 2 · Modules 2-1 to 2-6

Motion along a straight line

2-1Position, displacement and average velocity

  • Displacement Δx=x2−x1\Delta x=x_2-x_1Δx=x2​−x1​ has a sign; the distance is the total length of the path.
  • Average velocity is displacement over time, the slope of the secant on the xxx–ttt graph: vavg=ΔxΔtv_\text{avg}=\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}vavg​=ΔtΔx​
  • Average speed is the total distance over the time, so it is never negative.
Worked example2-1

A car drives 606060 km east in 1.01.01.0 h, then 303030 km west in 0.500.500.50 h. Take east as +x+x+x.

  1. (a)Find the displacement and the total distance.
  2. (b)Find the average velocity.
  3. (c)Find the average speed.
Show solutionHide solution
Answer
  • (a)+30+30+30 km (303030 km east);  90\ 90 90 km
  • (b)+20+20+20 km/h (202020 km/h east)
  • (c)606060 km/h

(a) Δx=+60−30=+30\Delta x=+60-30=+30Δx=+60−30=+30 km. The distance adds the legs without signs: 60+30=9060+30=9060+30=90 km.

(b) The trip takes 1.51.51.5 h in all: vavg=+30 km1.5 h=+20\displaystyle v_\text{avg}=\frac{+30\text{ km}}{1.5\text{ h}}=+20vavg​=1.5 h+30 km​=+20 km/h.

(c) savg=90 km1.5 h=60\displaystyle s_\text{avg}=\frac{90\text{ km}}{1.5\text{ h}}=60savg​=1.5 h90 km​=60 km/h. It is larger than ∣vavg∣|v_\text{avg}|∣vavg​∣ because the car turned back.

2-2Instantaneous velocity and speed

  • Instantaneous velocity is the derivative of position, the slope of the tangent on the xxx–ttt graph: v=dxdtv=\frac{dx}{dt}v=dtdx​
  • Speed is its size, ∣v∣|v|∣v∣. The particle is momentarily at rest where v=0v=0v=0.
Worked example2-2

A particle moves along the xxx-axis with x(t)=5+12t−2t3x(t)=5+12t-2t^3x(t)=5+12t−2t3 (xxx in metres, ttt in seconds).

  1. (a)Find v(t)v(t)v(t).
  2. (b)Find the velocity at t=1.0t=1.0t=1.0 s and the speed at t=2.0t=2.0t=2.0 s.
  3. (c)When is the particle momentarily at rest?
Show solutionHide solution
Answer
  • (a)v=12−6t2v=12-6t^2v=12−6t2 (m/s)
  • (b)6.06.06.0 m/s;  12\ 12 12 m/s
  • (c)At t=2≈1.4t=\sqrt{2}\approx1.4t=2​≈1.4 s

(a) Differentiate term by term: v=dxdt=0+12−6t2.\displaystyle v=\frac{dx}{dt}=0+12-6t^2.v=dtdx​=0+12−6t2.

(b) v(1)=12−6=6.0v(1)=12-6=6.0v(1)=12−6=6.0 m/s. v(2)=12−24=−12v(2)=12-24=-12v(2)=12−24=−12 m/s, so the speed is ∣v∣=12|v|=12∣v∣=12 m/s, moving in the −x-x−x direction.

(c) 12−6t2=012-6t^2=012−6t2=0 gives t2=2t^2=2t2=2, so t=2t=\sqrt{2}t=2​ s. The negative root is before the motion starts.

2-3Acceleration

  • Acceleration is the derivative of velocity: a=dvdt=d2xdt2,aavg=ΔvΔta=\frac{dv}{dt}=\frac{d^2x}{dt^2},\qquad a_\text{avg}=\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}a=dtdv​=dt2d2x​,aavg​=ΔtΔv​
  • Speeding up or slowing down: the same sign for vvv and aaa means speeding up, opposite signs mean slowing down. A negative aaa alone doesn't mean slowing down.
Worked example2-3

A particle moves with x(t)=5+12t−2t3x(t)=5+12t-2t^3x(t)=5+12t−2t3 (SI units), so its velocity is v(t)=12−6t2v(t)=12-6t^2v(t)=12−6t2.

  1. (a)Find a(t)a(t)a(t).
  2. (b)Find the average acceleration from t=0t=0t=0 to t=2.0t=2.0t=2.0 s.
  3. (c)At t=1.0t=1.0t=1.0 s and at t=2.0t=2.0t=2.0 s, is the particle speeding up or slowing down?
Show solutionHide solution
Answer
  • (a)a=−12ta=-12ta=−12t (m/s²)
  • (b)−12 m/s2-12\text{ m/s}^2−12 m/s2
  • (c)Slowing down at 1.01.01.0 s; speeding up at 2.02.02.0 s

(a) a=dvdt=−12t.\displaystyle a=\frac{dv}{dt}=-12t.a=dtdv​=−12t.

(b) aavg=v(2)−v(0)2−0=−12−122=−12 m/s2.\displaystyle a_\text{avg}=\frac{v(2)-v(0)}{2-0}=\frac{-12-12}{2}=-12\text{ m/s}^2.aavg​=2−0v(2)−v(0)​=2−12−12​=−12 m/s2. It equals a(1)a(1)a(1), the value at the middle of the interval, because aaa changes linearly.

(c) At t=1t=1t=1: v=6v=6v=6 m/s and a=−12 m/s2,a=-12\text{ m/s}^2,a=−12 m/s2, opposite signs, so it is slowing down. At t=2t=2t=2: v=−12v=-12v=−12 m/s and a=−24 m/s2,a=-24\text{ m/s}^2,a=−24 m/s2, the same sign, so it is speeding up in the −x-x−x direction.

2-4Constant acceleration

  • Five equations hold for constant acceleration, each without one of x−x0x-x_0x−x0​, vvv, v0v_0v0​, aaa and ttt: v=v0+atx−x0=v0t+12at2v2=v02+2a(x−x0)x−x0=12(v0+v)tx−x0=vt−12at2\begin{aligned}v&=v_0+at\\x-x_0&=v_0t+\tfrac{1}{2}at^2\\v^2&=v_0^2+2a(x-x_0)\\x-x_0&=\tfrac{1}{2}(v_0+v)t\\x-x_0&=vt-\tfrac{1}{2}at^2\end{aligned}vx−x0​v2x−x0​x−x0​​=v0​+at=v0​t+21​at2=v02​+2a(x−x0​)=21​(v0​+v)t=vt−21​at2​
  • Choosing one: list what you know and what you want, then use the equation without the quantity that is neither.
Worked example2-4

A car moving at 202020 m/s brakes with constant deceleration and stops in 404040 m.

  1. (a)Find its acceleration.
  2. (b)How long does it take to stop?
  3. (c)How far does it travel in the first 2.02.02.0 s of braking?

Answer
  • (a)−5.0 m/s2-5.0\text{ m/s}^2−5.0 m/s2
  • (b)4.04.04.0 s
  • (c)303030 m

(a) No time is given or asked, so use v2=v02+2a(x−x0)v^2=v_0^2+2a(x-x_0)v2=v02​+2a(x−x0​): 0=202+2a(40)0=20^2+2a(40)0=202+2a(40), so a=−40080=−5.0 m/s2.\displaystyle a=-\frac{400}{80}=-5.0\text{ m/s}^2.a=−80400​=−5.0 m/s2.

(b) v=v0+atv=v_0+atv=v0​+at: 0=20−5.0t0=20-5.0t0=20−5.0t, so t=4.0t=4.0t=4.0 s.

(c) x−x0=v0t+12at2=20(2.0)−12(5.0)(2.0)2=40−10=30\displaystyle x-x_0=v_0t+\frac{1}{2}at^2=20(2.0)-\frac{1}{2}(5.0)(2.0)^2=40-10=30x−x0​=v0​t+21​at2=20(2.0)−21​(5.0)(2.0)2=40−10=30 m: three quarters of the stopping distance in the first half of the time.

2-5Free-fall acceleration

  • Free fall is constant acceleration with a=−ga=-ga=−g (yyy up, g=9.8 m/s2g=9.8\text{ m/s}^2g=9.8 m/s2), the same for every mass when air is ignored.
  • At the top v=0v=0v=0, but the acceleration is still −g-g−g. The way down mirrors the way up: the same time, and the same speed at each height.

  • (b)v=−9.8v=-9.8v=−9.8 m/s (falling);  y=14.7\ y=14.7 y=14.7 m

Set up The acceleration is a=−ga=-ga=−g throughout, so the constant-acceleration equations apply with v0=19.6v_0=19.6v0​=19.6 m/s.

(c) y=0y=0y=0: t(19.6−4.9t)=0t(19.6-4.9t)=0t(19.6−4.9t)=0, so t=4.0t=4.0t=4.0 s, twice the time up. Then v=19.6−9.8(4.0)=−19.6v=19.6-9.8(4.0)=-19.6v=19.6−9.8(4.0)=−19.6 m/s: the launch speed, pointing down.

2-6Graphical integration

  • Slopes and areas: the slope of the xxx–ttt graph is vvv and the slope of the vvv–ttt graph is aaa. Going back, areas add up: v1−v0=∫t0t1a dt,x1−x0=∫t0t1v dtv_1-v_0=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}a\,dt,\qquad x_1-x_0=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}v\,dtv1​−v0​=∫t0​t1​​adt,x1​−x0​=∫t0​t1​​vdt
  • Signed areas: area below the time axis counts as negative.
Worked example2-6

An object starts from rest at x=0x=0x=0. Its acceleration is shown in the graph: 2.0 m/s22.0\text{ m/s}^22.0 m/s2 from 000 to 3.03.03.0 s, zero from 3.03.03.0 to 5.05.05.0 s, and −3.0 m/s2-3.0\text{ m/s}^2−3.0 m/s2 from 5.05.05.0 to 7.07.07.0 s.

  1. (a)Find the velocity at t=3.0t=3.0t=3.0, 5.05.05.0 and 7.07.07.0 s, and sketch the vvv–ttt graph.
  2. (b)Find the position at t=7.0t=7.0t=7.0 s.

Answer
  • (a)6.06.06.0, 6.06.06.0 and 000 m/s: up a straight line to 6.06.06.0 m/s, level, then down to 000
  • (b)x=27x=27x=27 m

(a) Each area under the aaa–ttt graph is a change in velocity: 2.0×3.0=+6.02.0\times3.0=+6.02.0×3.0=+6.0 m/s, then 000, then −3.0×2.0=−6.0-3.0\times2.0=-6.0−3.0×2.0=−6.0 m/s. So v=6.0v=6.0v=6.0 m/s at 3.03.03.0 s, still 6.06.06.0 m/s at 5.05.05.0 s, and 000 at 7.07.07.0 s.

(b) The area under the vvv–ttt graph is the displacement: 12(3.0)(6.0)+(2.0)(6.0)+12(2.0)(6.0)=9+12+6=27\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}(3.0)(6.0)+(2.0)(6.0)+\frac{1}{2}(2.0)(6.0)=9+12+6=2721​(3.0)(6.0)+(2.0)(6.0)+21​(2.0)(6.0)=9+12+6=27 m.

Watch out

  • Using the constant-acceleration equations when aaa changes with time. Differentiate or integrate instead.
  • A double minus: writing g=−9.8 m/s2g=-9.8\text{ m/s}^2g=−9.8 m/s2 and then a=−ga=-ga=−g. Keep ggg positive.
  • Displacement and distance differ once the object turns around: split the motion where v=0v=0v=0.

Chapter 3 · Modules 3-1 to 3-3

Vectors

3-1Vectors and their components

  • Components: a vector of magnitude aaa at angle θ\thetaθ, counterclockwise from +x+x+x, has ax=acos⁡θ,ay=asin⁡θa_x=a\cos\theta,\qquad a_y=a\sin\thetaax​=acosθ,ay​=asinθ
  • Back again: a=ax2+ay2a=\sqrt{a_x^2+a_y^2}a=ax2​+ay2​​ and tan⁡θ=ayax.\tan\theta=\frac{a_y}{a_x}.tanθ=ax​ay​​. When ax<0a_x<0ax​<0, add 180∘180^\circ180∘ to what tan⁡−1\tan^{-1}tan−1 gives.

Chapter 4 · Modules 4-1 to 4-7

Motion in two and three dimensions

4-1Position and displacement

  • The position vector r⃗=xi^+yj^+zk^\vec{r}=x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}+z\hat{k}r=xi^+yj^​+zk^ points from the origin to the particle.
  • Displacement Δr⃗=r⃗2−r⃗1\Delta\vec{r}=\vec{r}_2-\vec{r}_1Δr=r2​−r1​: subtract each component.

4-2Average and instantaneous velocity

  • Velocity is the derivative of the position vector, one component at a time, and is always tangent to the path: v⃗=dr⃗dt=dxdti^+dydtj^+dzdtk^\vec{v}=\frac{d\vec{r}}{dt}=\frac{dx}{dt}\hat{i}+\frac{dy}{dt}\hat{j}+\frac{dz}{dt}\hat{k}v=dtdr​=dtdx​i^+dtdy​j^​+dtdz​k^
  • Average velocity v⃗avg=Δr⃗Δt\vec{v}_\text{avg}=\frac{\Delta\vec{r}}{\Delta t}vavg​=ΔtΔr​ points along the displacement.

4-3Average and instantaneous acceleration

  • Acceleration is the derivative of the velocity vector: a⃗=dv⃗dt=dvxdti^+dvydtj^+dvzdtk^\vec{a}=\frac{d\vec{v}}{dt}=\frac{dv_x}{dt}\hat{i}+\frac{dv_y}{dt}\hat{j}+\frac{dv_z}{dt}\hat{k}a=dtdv​=dtdvx​​i^+dtdvy​​j^​+dtdvz​​k^
  • Speeding up or slowing down: look at v⃗⋅a⃗.\vec{v}\cdot\vec{a}.v⋅a. Positive means speeding up, negative slowing down, and zero means only the direction is turning at that moment.

  • Two motions at once: horizontally a constant velocity v0cos⁡θ0v_0\cos\theta_0v0​cosθ0​, vertically free fall starting at v0sin⁡θ0v_0\sin\theta_0v0​sinθ0​. The time ttt links them: x−x0=(v0cos⁡θ0) ty−y0=(v0sin⁡θ0) t−12gt2\begin{gathered}x-x_0=(v_0\cos\theta_0)\,t\\y-y_0=(v_0\sin\theta_0)\,t-\tfrac{1}{2}gt^2\end{gathered}x−x0​=(v0​cosθ0​)ty−y0​=(v0​sinθ0​)t−21​gt2​

4-5Uniform circular motion

  • Constant speed, turning direction: the velocity changes, so there is an acceleration, and it points to the centre: a=v2r,T=2πrva=\frac{v^2}{r},\qquad T=\frac{2\pi r}{v}a=rv2​,T=v2πr​
  • Twice the speed gives four times the acceleration.

A car drives around a circular track of radius 505050 m at a constant 101010 m/s.

  1. (a)Find its acceleration.
  2. (b)How long does one lap take?
  3. (c)What would the acceleration be at 202020 m/s?

  • (a)2.0 m/s22.0\text{ m/s}^22.0 m/s2, toward the centre
  • (b)10π≈3110\pi\approx3110π≈31 s

(a) a=v2r=10250=2.0 m/s2,\displaystyle a=\frac{v^2}{r}=\frac{10^2}{50}=2.0\text{ m/s}^2,a=rv2​=50102​=2.0 m/s2, pointing to the centre of the track.

(b) One lap is 2πr2\pi r2πr long: T=2π(50)10=10π\displaystyle T=\frac{2\pi(50)}{10}=10\piT=102π(50)​=10π s.

(c) aaa grows with v2v^2v2: 20250=8.0 m/s2,\displaystyle \frac{20^2}{50}=8.0\text{ m/s}^2,50202​=8.0 m/s2, four times as much.

4-6Relative motion in one dimension

  • Velocities add, with the subscripts chaining: the velocity of PPP relative to AAA is vPA=vPB+vBAv_{PA}=v_{PB}+v_{BA}vPA​=vPB​+vBA​ and reversing the order flips the sign, vAB=−vBAv_{AB}=-v_{BA}vAB​=−vBA​.
  • Accelerations agree in frames that move at constant velocity relative to each other: aPA=aPBa_{PA}=a_{PB}aPA​=aPB​.
Worked example4-6

A train moves east at 202020 m/s. A passenger walks toward the back of the train at 1.51.51.5 m/s relative to the train. Take east as positive.

  1. (a)Find the passenger's velocity relative to the ground.

Answer
  • (a)+18.5+18.5+18.5 m/s (east)

(a) vPG=vPT+vTG=−1.5+20=+18.5v_{PG}=v_{PT}+v_{TG}=-1.5+20=+18.5vPG​=vPT​+vTG​=−1.5+20=+18.5 m/s.

(b) vPC=vPG+vGC,v_{PC}=v_{PG}+v_{GC},vPC​=vPG​+vGC​, with vGC=−vCG=−25v_{GC}=-v_{CG}=-25vGC​=−vCG​=−25 m/s: vPC=18.5−25=−6.5v_{PC}=18.5-25=-6.5vPC​=18.5−25=−6.5 m/s. Seen from the faster car, the passenger moves backward.

4-7Relative motion in two dimensions

  • The same rule with vectors: v⃗PA=v⃗PB+v⃗BA.\vec{v}_{PA}=\vec{v}_{PB}+\vec{v}_{BA}.vPA​=vPB​+vBA​. Add by components, or with a right-angle triangle when the two parts are perpendicular.
  • River crossings: the boat's velocity over the ground is its velocity through the water plus the water's velocity.
Worked example4-7

A river 808080 m wide flows at 3.03.03.0 m/s. A boat moves at 4.04.04.0 m/s relative to the water, heading straight across.

  1. (a)Find the boat's velocity relative to the ground.
  2. (b)How long does the crossing take, and how far downstream does the boat land?
  3. (c)A faster boat moves at 5.05.05.0 m/s relative to the water. Which way must it head to land straight across, and how long does that take?
Show solutionHide solution
Answer
  • (a)5.05.05.0 m/s, at 37∘37^\circ37∘ downstream from straight across
  • (b)202020 s;  60\ 60 60 m
  • (c)37∘37^\circ37∘ upstream from straight across;  20\ 20 20 s

(a) v⃗BG=v⃗BW+v⃗WG\vec{v}_{BG}=\vec{v}_{BW}+\vec{v}_{WG}vBG​=vBW​+vWG​: 4.04.04.0 m/s across plus 3.03.03.0 m/s downstream, at right angles. ∣v⃗BG∣=4.02+3.02=5.0|\vec{v}_{BG}|=\sqrt{4.0^2+3.0^2}=5.0∣vBG​∣=4.02+3.02​=5.0 m/s, at tan⁡−13.04.0=37∘\displaystyle \tan^{-1}\frac{3.0}{4.0}=37^\circtan−14.03.0​=37∘ from straight across.

(b) Only the across part carries the boat over: t=804.0=20\displaystyle t=\frac{80}{4.0}=20t=4.080​=20 s. Meanwhile the current carries it 3.0×20=603.0\times20=603.0×20=60 m downstream.

(c) Its upstream part must cancel the current: 5.0sin⁡α=3.0,5.0\sin\alpha=3.0,5.0sinα=3.0, so sin⁡α=0.60\sin\alpha=0.60sinα=0.60 and α=37∘\alpha=37^\circα=37∘ upstream. The across part is 5.0cos⁡37∘=4.05.0\cos37^\circ=4.05.0cos37∘=4.0 m/s, so the crossing again takes 202020 s.

Watch out

  • The range formula only holds when the projectile lands at its launch height.

Chapter 5 · Modules 5-1 to 5-3

Force and motion I

5-1Newton’s first and second laws

  • First law: with no net force, a body keeps its velocity; at rest, it stays at rest.
  • Second law, for each axis separately: F⃗net=ma⃗\vec{F}_\text{net}=m\vec{a}Fnet​=ma Forces add as vectors, and 1 N=1 kg⋅m/s2.1\text{ N}=1\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}^2.1 N=1 kg⋅m/s2.

5-2Some particular forces

  • The gravitational force Fg=mgF_g=mgFg​=mg points down; the weight W=mgW=mgW=mg is its size.
  • The normal force is perpendicular to the surface and only as large as needed. It equals mgmgmg only on a level surface with no other vertical forces and no vertical acceleration.

5-3Applying Newton’s laws

  • Method: draw a free-body diagram for each body, choose axes (along and across a slope), write Fnet=maF_\text{net}=maFnet​=ma for each axis, then solve. Bodies tied by a string share the size of their acceleration.
  • On an incline, gravity splits into mgsin⁡θmg\sin\thetamgsinθ down the slope and mgcos⁡θmg\cos\thetamgcosθ into it; the normal force balances the second part.
  • Third law: F⃗BC=−F⃗CB,\vec{F}_{BC}=-\vec{F}_{CB},FBC​=−FCB​, two forces on two different bodies.

A 5.05.05.0 kg box is pulled up a frictionless ramp at 30∘30^\circ30∘ by a cord parallel to the ramp, with a tension of 404040 N. Take g=9.8 m/s2.g=9.8\text{ m/s}^2.g=9.8 m/s2.

Chapter 6 · Modules 6-1 to 6-3

Force and motion II

6-1Friction

  • Static friction holds a body still and is only as large as needed, up to fs,max⁡=μsFN,f_{s,\max}=\mu_sF_N,fs,max​=μs​FN​, which it reaches just as sliding starts.
  • Kinetic friction acts once the body slides: fk=μkFNf_k=\mu_kF_Nfk​=μk​FN​, against the motion, usually smaller since μk<μs\mu_k<\mu_sμk​<μs​.
  • Friction depends on the normal force, so find FNF_NFN​ first.
Worked example6-1

A 5.05.05.0 kg crate is placed on a ramp at 37∘37^\circ37∘, with μs=0.50\mu_s=0.50μs​=0.50 and μk=0.25\mu_k=0.25μk​=0.25. Take g=9.8 m/s2.g=9.8\text{ m/s}^2.g=9.8 m/s2. Use sin⁡37∘≈0.60\sin37^\circ\approx0.60sin37∘≈0.60 and cos⁡37∘≈0.80.\cos37^\circ\approx0.80.cos37∘≈0.80.

  4. (d)What force up along the ramp starts it moving up the ramp?

  • (b)3.92 m/s23.92\text{ m/s}^23.92 m/s2

Set up mg=49mg=49mg=49 N. Along the ramp gravity pulls down with mgsin⁡37∘=29.4mg\sin37^\circ=29.4mgsin37∘=29.4 N; into the ramp it presses with mgcos⁡37∘=39.2mg\cos37^\circ=39.2mgcos37∘=39.2 N, so FN=39.2F_N=39.2FN​=39.2 N.

  • A net force toward the centre keeps a body moving on a circle: Fnet=mv2RF_\text{net}=\frac{mv^2}{R}Fnet​=Rmv2​ It is not a new force: friction, tension, the normal force or gravity, or a mix, provides it.

7-1Kinetic energy

  • Kinetic energy is the energy of motion, a scalar measured in joules (1 J=1 kg⋅m2/s21\text{ J}=1\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}^21 J=1 kg⋅m2/s2): K=12mv2K=\frac{1}{2}mv^2K=21​mv2
  • Twice the speed means four times the kinetic energy.

7-2Work and kinetic energy

  • Work by a constant force is the part of the force along the motion times the distance: W=Fdcos⁡ϕ=F⃗⋅d⃗W=Fd\cos\phi=\vec{F}\cdot\vec{d}W=Fdcosϕ=F⋅d It is positive when the force helps the motion, negative when it opposes it, and zero when the force is perpendicular.
  • Work–kinetic energy theorem: the net work changes the kinetic energy, ΔK=Kf−Ki=Wnet.\Delta K=K_f-K_i=W_\text{net}.ΔK=Kf​−Ki​=Wnet​.

(b) Ws=12k(xi2−xf2)=200(0.0502−0.152)=200(0.0025−0.0225)=−4.0\displaystyle W_s=\frac{1}{2}k\left(x_i^2-x_f^2\right)=200\left(0.050^2-0.15^2\right)=200(0.0025-0.0225)=-4.0Ws​=21​k(xi2​−xf2​)=200(0.0502−0.152)=200(0.0025−0.0225)=−4.0 J: the spring pulls against the stretch.

(c) At rest before and after, so Wa=−Ws=+4.0W_a=-W_s=+4.0Wa​=−Ws​=+4.0 J.

(d) Now xi=0.15x_i=0.15xi​=0.15 m and xf=0.050x_f=0.050xf​=0.050 m: Ws=200(0.0225−0.0025)=+4.0W_s=200(0.0225-0.0025)=+4.0Ws​=200(0.0225−0.0025)=+4.0 J.

7-5Work done by a general variable force

  • A variable force does work W=∫xixfF(x) dxW=\int_{x_i}^{x_f}F(x)\,dxW=∫xi​xf​​F(x)dx the area under the FFF–xxx graph, counted negative below the axis.
  • The work–kinetic energy theorem still holds: ΔK=W\Delta K=WΔK=W.
Worked example7-5

A force F(x)=12−4xF(x)=12-4xF(x)=12−4x (in newtons, with xxx in metres) acts along the xxx-axis on a 2.02.02.0 kg object that starts from rest at x=0x=0x=0. No other force does work.

  1. (a)Find the work done from x=0x=0x=0 to x=2.0x=2.0x=2.0 m.
  2. (b)Find the speed at x=2.0x=2.0x=2.0 m.
  3. (c)Where is the object fastest, and how fast is it there?
  4. (d)Where does it stop?
Show solutionHide solution
Answer
  • (a)161616 J
  • (b)4.04.04.0 m/s
  • (c)At x=3.0x=3.0x=3.0 m, 32≈4.23\sqrt{2}\approx4.232​≈4.2 m/s
  • (d)At x=6.0x=6.0x=6.0 m

(a) W=∫02(12−4x) dx=[12x−2x2]02=24−8=16W=\int_0^2(12-4x)\,dx=\left[12x-2x^2\right]_0^2=24-8=16W=∫02​(12−4x)dx=[12x−2x2]02​=24−8=16 J: the trapezoid under the line.

(b) 12(2.0)v2=16,\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}(2.0)v^2=16,21​(2.0)v2=16, so v=4.0v=4.0v=4.0 m/s.

(c) It speeds up while F>0F>0F>0 and slows down after, so it is fastest where F=0F=0F=0: x=3.0x=3.0x=3.0 m. There W=36−18=18W=36-18=18W=36−18=18 J, so v2=18v^2=18v2=18 and v=32v=3\sqrt{2}v=32​ m/s.

(d) K=W=12x−2x2=2x(6−x)K=W=12x-2x^2=2x(6-x)K=W=12x−2x2=2x(6−x) is zero again at x=6.0x=6.0x=6.0 m: the negative area beyond x=3x=3x=3 m cancels the positive area before it.

7-6Power

  • Power is the rate of doing work: Pavg=WΔt,P=dWdt=Fvcos⁡ϕP_\text{avg}=\frac{W}{\Delta t},\qquad P=\frac{dW}{dt}=Fv\cos\phiPavg​=ΔtW​,P=dtdW​=Fvcosϕ in watts, 1 W=1 J/s.1\text{ W}=1\text{ J/s}.1 W=1 J/s. Also 1 hp=7461\text{ hp}=7461 hp=746 W, and 1 kW⋅h=3.6×1061\text{ kW}\cdot\text{h}=3.6\times10^61 kW⋅h=3.6×106 J is an energy.
Worked example7-6

A 120012001200 kg car speeds up from rest to 202020 m/s in 8.08.08.0 s on a level road, with constant acceleration. Ignore friction and air during this part.

  1. (a)How much work does the net force do?
  2. (b)Find the average power.
  3. (c)Find the power delivered at the end of the 8.08.08.0 s.
  4. (d)The car then cruises at 202020 m/s against a drag force of 500500500 N. What power must the engine deliver?
Show solutionHide solution
Answer
  • (a)2.4×1052.4\times10^52.4×105 J
  • (b)3.0×1043.0\times10^43.0×104 W (303030 kW)
  • (c)6.0×1046.0\times10^46.0×104 W (606060 kW)
  • (d)1.0×1041.0\times10^41.0×104 W (101010 kW)

(a) Work–kinetic energy theorem: W=ΔK=12(1200)(20)2−0=2.4×105\displaystyle W=\Delta K=\frac{1}{2}(1200)(20)^2-0=2.4\times10^5W=ΔK=21​(1200)(20)2−0=2.4×105 J.

(b) Pavg=WΔt=2.4×1058.0=3.0×104\displaystyle P_\text{avg}=\frac{W}{\Delta t}=\frac{2.4\times10^5}{8.0}=3.0\times10^4Pavg​=ΔtW​=8.02.4×105​=3.0×104 W.

(c) a=208.0=2.5 m/s2,\displaystyle a=\frac{20}{8.0}=2.5\text{ m/s}^2,a=8.020​=2.5 m/s2, so the net force is F=ma=3000F=ma=3000F=ma=3000 N. At 202020 m/s, P=Fv=3000×20=6.0×104P=Fv=3000\times20=6.0\times10^4P=Fv=3000×20=6.0×104 W: twice the average, because the speed rose steadily from zero.

(d) At a constant speed the engine's force balances the drag, 500500500 N: P=Fv=500×20=1.0×104P=Fv=500\times20=1.0\times10^4P=Fv=500×20=1.0×104 W.

Watch out

  • ϕ\phiϕ is the angle between the force and the displacement, which is not always the angle given in the problem.
  • A force perpendicular to the motion, such as the normal force or a centripetal force, does no work.
  • The sign of spring work: positive when the spring moves back toward its relaxed length, negative when it is stretched or compressed further.

Chapter 8 · Modules 8-1 to 8-5

Potential energy and conservation of energy

8-1Potential energy

  • Potential energy stores the work of a conservative force: ΔU=−W\Delta U=-WΔU=−W. Gravity: U=mgyU=mgyU=mgy. A spring: U=12kx2.U=\frac{1}{2}kx^2.U=21​kx2.
  • Only changes matter, so choose where U=0U=0U=0 (the floor, the relaxed spring) to suit the problem.
Worked example8-1

Take g=9.8 m/s2.g=9.8\text{ m/s}^2.g=9.8 m/s2.

  1. (a)A 2.02.02.0 kg book is lifted from the floor to a shelf 1.51.51.5 m higher. Find the change in its gravitational potential energy.
  2. (b)Taking U=0U=0U=0 at the shelf instead, what is the book's potential energy on the floor?
  3. (c)A spring with k=800k=800k=800 N/m is compressed by 5.05.05.0 cm. Find its elastic potential energy.
  4. (d)Find the change in elastic potential energy when the compression goes from 5.05.05.0 cm to 101010 cm.
Show solutionHide solution
Answer
  • (a)+29.4+29.4+29.4 J
  • (b)−29.4-29.4−29.4 J
  • (c)1.01.01.0 J
  • (d)+3.0+3.0+3.0 J

(a) ΔU=mg Δy=2.0(9.8)(1.5)=29.4\Delta U=mg\,\Delta y=2.0(9.8)(1.5)=29.4ΔU=mgΔy=2.0(9.8)(1.5)=29.4 J. Gravity did −29.4-29.4−29.4 J of work.

(b) The floor is 1.51.51.5 m below the shelf: U=mgy=2.0(9.8)(−1.5)=−29.4U=mgy=2.0(9.8)(-1.5)=-29.4U=mgy=2.0(9.8)(−1.5)=−29.4 J. The change between the two places is still 29.429.429.4 J.

(c) U=12kx2=12(800)(0.050)2=1.0\displaystyle U=\frac{1}{2}kx^2=\frac{1}{2}(800)(0.050)^2=1.0U=21​kx2=21​(800)(0.050)2=1.0 J.

(d) 12(800)(0.10)2=4.0\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}(800)(0.10)^2=4.021​(800)(0.10)2=4.0 J, so ΔU=4.0−1.0=+3.0\Delta U=4.0-1.0=+3.0ΔU=4.0−1.0=+3.0 J: twice the compression stores four times the energy.

8-2Conservation of mechanical energy

  • Mechanical energy Emec=K+UE_\text{mec}=K+UEmec​=K+U stays constant when only conservative forces (gravity, springs) do work: K2+U2=K1+U1K_2+U_2=K_1+U_1K2​+U2​=K1​+U1​
  • It links speeds and positions without the path or the time.
Worked example8-2

A 0.200.200.20 kg block is pressed against a spring (k=980k=980k=980 N/m), compressing it by 0.100.100.10 m on a frictionless level track. Released, it leaves the spring and slides up a frictionless ramp. Take g=9.8 m/s2.g=9.8\text{ m/s}^2.g=9.8 m/s2.

  1. (a)Find the block's speed as it leaves the spring.
  2. (b)How high up the ramp does it go?
  3. (c)Find its speed at half that height.
  4. (d)It slides back down into the spring. How far does it compress it?
Show solutionHide solution
Answer
  • (a)7.07.07.0 m/s
  • (b)2.52.52.5 m
  • (c)7.02≈4.9\displaystyle \frac{7.0}{\sqrt{2}}\approx4.92​7.0​≈4.9 m/s
  • (d)0.100.100.10 m

Set up Nothing removes energy, so K+Uspring+UgravK+U_\text{spring}+U_\text{grav}K+Uspring​+Ugrav​ stays constant. At the start it is all elastic: 12kx2=12(980)(0.10)2=4.9\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}kx^2=\frac{1}{2}(980)(0.10)^2=4.921​kx2=21​(980)(0.10)2=4.9 J.

(a) 12mv2=4.9\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}mv^2=4.921​mv2=4.9 J, so v2=2(4.9)0.20=49\displaystyle v^2=\frac{2(4.9)}{0.20}=49v2=0.202(4.9)​=49 and v=7.0v=7.0v=7.0 m/s.

(b) At the highest point it is all gravitational: mgh=4.9mgh=4.9mgh=4.9 J, so h=4.90.20(9.8)=2.5\displaystyle h=\frac{4.9}{0.20(9.8)}=2.5h=0.20(9.8)4.9​=2.5 m.

(c) At h=1.25h=1.25h=1.25 m half the energy is gravitational and half kinetic: 12mv2=2.45\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}mv^2=2.4521​mv2=2.45 J, so v2=24.5v^2=24.5v2=24.5 and v=7.02≈4.9\displaystyle v=\frac{7.0}{\sqrt{2}}\approx4.9v=2​7.0​≈4.9 m/s.

(d) Coming back, all 4.94.94.9 J become elastic energy again, so it compresses the spring by 0.100.100.10 m: nothing has been lost.

8-3Reading a potential energy curve

  • Force from the curve: F(x)=−dUdx,F(x)=-\frac{dU}{dx},F(x)=−dxdU​, minus the slope.
  • Where the particle can go: K=Emec−U≥0,K=E_\text{mec}-U\ge0,K=Emec​−U≥0, so it stays where U≤EmecU\le E_\text{mec}U≤Emec​ and turns around where U=EmecU=E_\text{mec}U=Emec​.
  • Equilibrium is where the slope is zero: a minimum of UUU is stable, a maximum unstable.
Worked example8-3

A particle moving along the xxx-axis has potential energy U(x)=x2−4x+5U(x)=x^2-4x+5U(x)=x2−4x+5 (UUU in joules, xxx in metres) and mechanical energy Emec=5E_\text{mec}=5Emec​=5 J.

  1. (a)Find the force F(x)F(x)F(x) on the particle.
  2. (b)Where is the equilibrium point, and is it stable or unstable?
  3. (c)Find the turning points.
  4. (d)Where is the particle fastest, and what is its kinetic energy there?
Show solutionHide solution
Answer
  • (a)F(x)=4−2xF(x)=4-2xF(x)=4−2x (N)
  • (b)At x=2x=2x=2 m, stable
  • (c)x=0x=0x=0 and x=4x=4x=4 m
  • (d)At x=2x=2x=2 m, with K=4K=4K=4 J

(a) F(x)=−dUdx=−(2x−4)=4−2x.\displaystyle F(x)=-\frac{dU}{dx}=-(2x-4)=4-2x.F(x)=−dxdU​=−(2x−4)=4−2x.

(b) Equilibrium is where F=0F=0F=0: x=2x=2x=2 m. There U=4−8+5=1U=4-8+5=1U=4−8+5=1 J, the minimum of an upward parabola, so it is stable: the force points back toward x=2x=2x=2 from both sides.

(c) It turns around where U=EmecU=E_\text{mec}U=Emec​: x2−4x+5=5x^2-4x+5=5x2−4x+5=5, so x(x−4)=0x(x-4)=0x(x−4)=0, at x=0x=0x=0 and x=4x=4x=4 m. It moves back and forth between them.

(d) K=Emec−UK=E_\text{mec}-UK=Emec​−U is largest where UUU is smallest, at x=2x=2x=2 m: K=5−1=4K=5-1=4K=5−1=4 J.

8-4Work done on a system by an external force

  • External work changes a system's energy. Without friction, W=ΔK+ΔUW=\Delta K+\Delta UW=ΔK+ΔU; with friction, W=ΔEmec+ΔEth,ΔEth=fkdW=\Delta E_\text{mec}+\Delta E_\text{th},\qquad \Delta E_\text{th}=f_kdW=ΔEmec​+ΔEth​,ΔEth​=fk​d
  • Kinetic friction turns mechanical energy into thermal energy of the surfaces.
Worked example8-4

A worker pushes a 4.04.04.0 kg block from rest across a level floor with a steady horizontal 19.619.619.6 N force for 5.05.05.0 m, then lets go. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.250.250.25; take g=9.8 m/s2.g=9.8\text{ m/s}^2.g=9.8 m/s2.

  1. (a)Find the work done by the worker.
  2. (b)Find the thermal energy produced during the push.
  3. (c)Find the block's kinetic energy when the worker lets go.
  4. (d)How much farther does it slide?
Show solutionHide solution
Answer
  • (a)989898 J
  • (b)494949 J
  • (c)494949 J
  • (d)5.05.05.0 m

Set up The friction force is fk=μkmg=0.25(4.0)(9.8)=9.8f_k=\mu_kmg=0.25(4.0)(9.8)=9.8fk​=μk​mg=0.25(4.0)(9.8)=9.8 N, against the motion.

(a) W=Fd=19.6(5.0)=98W=Fd=19.6(5.0)=98W=Fd=19.6(5.0)=98 J.

(b) ΔEth=fkd=9.8(5.0)=49\Delta E_\text{th}=f_kd=9.8(5.0)=49ΔEth​=fk​d=9.8(5.0)=49 J.

(c) On a level floor W=ΔK+ΔEth,W=\Delta K+\Delta E_\text{th},W=ΔK+ΔEth​, so ΔK=98−49=49\Delta K=98-49=49ΔK=98−49=49 J.

(d) Now friction turns those 494949 J into thermal energy: 9.8 d′=499.8\,d'=499.8d′=49, so d′=5.0d'=5.0d′=5.0 m.

8-5Conservation of energy

  • Energy is conserved: it is never created or destroyed. For an isolated system, ΔEmec+ΔEth+ΔEint=0\Delta E_\text{mec}+\Delta E_\text{th}+\Delta E_\text{int}=0ΔEmec​+ΔEth​+ΔEint​=0 so mechanical energy lost to friction or drag shows up as thermal energy.
  • Power is the energy transferred per unit time: Pavg=ΔEΔt.P_\text{avg}=\frac{\Delta E}{\Delta t}.Pavg​=ΔtΔE​.
Worked example8-5

A 0.500.500.50 kg ball is dropped from a height of 202020 m and hits the ground at 181818 m/s. Take g=9.8 m/s2.g=9.8\text{ m/s}^2.g=9.8 m/s2.

  1. (a)How much mechanical energy is lost to the air?
  2. (b)Find the average drag force during the fall.
  3. (c)How fast would it land with no air?
Show solutionHide solution
Answer
  • (a)171717 J
  • (b)0.850.850.85 N
  • (c)142≈2014\sqrt{2}\approx20142​≈20 m/s

(a) At the top Emec=mgh=0.50(9.8)(20)=98E_\text{mec}=mgh=0.50(9.8)(20)=98Emec​=mgh=0.50(9.8)(20)=98 J; at the bottom 12(0.50)(18)2=81\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}(0.50)(18)^2=8121​(0.50)(18)2=81 J. The difference, 171717 J, became thermal energy of the ball and the air.

(b) ΔEth=Dˉ d,\Delta E_\text{th}=\bar{D}\,d,ΔEth​=Dˉd, so Dˉ=1720=0.85\displaystyle \bar{D}=\frac{17}{20}=0.85Dˉ=2017​=0.85 N.

(c) With nothing lost, 12mv2=mgh\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}mv^2=mgh21​mv2=mgh: v=2(9.8)(20)=392=142≈20v=\sqrt{2(9.8)(20)}=\sqrt{392}=14\sqrt{2}\approx20v=2(9.8)(20)​=392​=142​≈20 m/s.

Watch out

  • Energy gives speeds and heights, not directions or times.
  • Leaving out a form of energy: count kinetic, gravitational and elastic energy at both points.
  • With friction, mechanical energy is not conserved, but total energy is: add ΔEth.\Delta E_\text{th}.ΔEth​.

Exam-day habits

  • Sketch first. Draw the situation and a free-body diagram, and choose a positive direction (up the slope, toward the centre) before writing any equation.
  • Symbols, then numbers. Solve in symbols and put the numbers in at the end; the mass often cancels.
  • No calculator. Keep exact forms such as 3\sqrt{3}3​ and π\piπ, use the special angles (sin⁡37∘≈0.6,\sin37^\circ\approx0.6,sin37∘≈0.6, cos⁡37∘≈0.8\cos37^\circ\approx0.8cos37∘≈0.8), and round only the final answer.
  • Units and signs. Write units on every number and check the unit of the answer. Keep g=9.8 m/s2g=9.8\text{ m/s}^2g=9.8 m/s2 positive and put the direction in the sign.
  • Check a special case. Setting θ=0\theta=0θ=0, μ=0\mu=0μ=0 or one mass to zero should give a result you already know.
